questions.question: Consider a permutation sampled uniformly at random from the set of all permutations of [latex]\{1,2,3, \cdots, n\} [/latex] for some [latex]n \geq 4 [/latex]. Let [latex]X [/latex] be the event that 1 occurs before 2 in the permutation, and [latex]Y [/latex] the event that 3 occurs before 4 . Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

options.A: The events [latex]X [/latex] and [latex]Y [/latex] are mutually exclusive
options.D: Event [latex]X [/latex] is more likely than event [latex]Y [/latex]

questions.explanation:
By symmetry, 1 is before 2 in half of all permutations, so [latex]P(X)=\frac12[/latex]; similarly [latex]P(Y)=\frac12[/latex].

The relative order of {1,2} and the relative order of {3,4} involve different elements, and all 4 combinations (12/21 with 34/43) are equally likely, so [latex]P(X\cap Y)=\frac14=P(X)P(Y)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] independent.

- Not mutually exclusive: 1 2 3 4 [latex]\ldots[/latex] satisfies both.
- Neither must occur: 2 1 4 3 [latex]\ldots[/latex] satisfies none.
- Equally likely, so X is not more likely than Y.

Answer: X and Y are independent

questions.question: Let [latex]A [/latex] and [latex]B [/latex] be non-empty finite sets such that there exist one-to-one and onto functions (i) from [latex]A [/latex] to [latex]B [/latex] and (ii) from [latex]A \times A [/latex] to [latex]A \cup B [/latex]. The number of possible values of [latex]|A| [/latex] is ___
questions.explanation:
Bijection [latex]A\to B[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]|A|=|B|=n[/latex].
Bijection [latex]A\times A\to A\cup B[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]n^2=|A\cup B|[/latex].

But [latex]n\le|A\cup B|\le 2n[/latex], so [latex]n\le n^2\le 2n[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]n\le2[/latex].

- [latex]n=1[/latex]: [latex]A=B[/latex], [latex]|A\cup B|=1=1^2[/latex] True
- [latex]n=2[/latex]: take A and B disjoint, [latex]|A\cup B|=4=2^2[/latex] True

So [latex]|A|\in\{1,2\}[/latex].

Answer: 2

questions.question:
Let p and q be two propositions. Consider the following two formulae in propositional logic.

[latex]S1: (\neg p\wedge(p\vee q))\rightarrow q[/latex]
[latex]S2: q\rightarrow(\neg p\wedge(p\vee q))[/latex]

Which one of the following choices is correct?

options.A: Both S1 and S2 are tautologies.
options.B: S1 is a tautology but S2 is not a tautology
options.C: S1 is not a tautology but S2 is a tautology
options.D: Niether S1 nor S2 is a tautology

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- S1: [latex] eg p\wedge(p\vee q)\equiv eg p\wedge q[/latex], and [latex]( eg p\wedge q) ightarrow q[/latex] is always true [latex] ightarrow[/latex] tautology.
- S2: take p = q = 1: q is true but [latex] eg p\wedge(p\vee q)[/latex] is false [latex] ightarrow[/latex] S2 is false [latex] ightarrow[/latex] not a tautology.

Answer: S1 is a tautology but S2 is not a tautology

questions.question:
Let [latex]U=\{1,2,,...n\}[/latex]. Let [latex]A=\{(x,X)|x\in X,X\subseteq U\}[/latex]. Consider the following two statements on |A|.

I. [latex]|A|=n2^{n-1}[/latex]
II. [latex]|A|=\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\binom{n}{k}[/latex]

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?
questions.explanation:
Count the pairs (x, X) with [latex]x\in X[/latex] in two ways:
- Fix x first: x lies in [latex]2^{n-1}[/latex] subsets, so [latex]|A|=n\,2^{n-1}[/latex].
- Fix the size k of X first: there are [latex]\binom nk[/latex] such sets, each giving k choices of x, so [latex]|A|=\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\binom nk[/latex].

Both are correct (and equal).

Answer: Both I and II

Answer: 0.503

questions.question: Let [latex]A [/latex] and [latex]B [/latex] be two events in a probability space with [latex]P(A)=0.3, P(B)=0.5 [/latex], and [latex]P(A \cap B)=0.1 [/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.A: The two events [latex]A [/latex] and [latex]B [/latex] are independent
options.C: [latex]P\left(A \cap B^c\right)=0.2 [/latex], where [latex]B^c [/latex] is the complement of the event [latex]B [/latex]
options.D: [latex]P\left(A^c \cap B^c\right)=0.4 [/latex], where [latex]A^c [/latex] and [latex]B^c [/latex] are the complements of the events [latex]A [/latex] and [latex]B [/latex], respectively

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Independence: [latex]P(A)P(B)=0.15\ne0.1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]P(A\cup B)=0.3+0.5-0.1=0.7[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]P(A\cap B^c)=P(A)-P(A\cap B)=0.3-0.1=0.2[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]P(A^c\cap B^c)=1-P(A\cup B)=0.3\ne0.4[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: [latex]P(A\cup B)=0.7[/latex] and [latex]P(A\cap B^c)=0.2[/latex]

questions.question: Let G be a graph with 100! vertices, with each vertex labelled by a distinct permutation of the numbers 1,2,...,100. - Adjacent swaps can produce every permutation (bubble sort), so the graph is connected [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] z = 1.

y + 10z = 99 + 10 = 109

questions.question: Let G be a group of order 6, and H be a subgroup of G such that 1 < |H| < 6. Which one of the following options is correct?

options.A: Both G and H are always cyclic.
options.B: G may not be cyclic, but H is always cyclic.
options.C: G is always cyclic, but H may not be cyclic.
options.D: Both G and H may not be cyclic.

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- G can be the non-abelian group [latex]S_3[/latex] (order 6), which is not cyclic.
- By Lagrange, |H| divides 6 and is strictly between 1 and 6, so |H| = 2 or 3, which are primes. Every group of prime order is cyclic.

Answer: G may not be cyclic, but H is always cyclic

questions.question:
Which of the following predicate logic formulae/formula is/are CORRECT representation(s) of the statement: "Everyone has exactly one mother"?

The meanings of the predicates used are:
[latex]mother(y,x): y[/latex] is the mother of [latex] x [/latex]
[latex]noteq(x,y): x[/latex] and [latex] y [/latex] are not equal

options.A: [latex] \forall x \exists y \exists z (mother(y, x) \land \neg mother(z, x)) [/latex]
options.B: [latex] \forall x \exists y [mother(y, x) \land \forall z (noteq(z, y) \to \neg mother(z, x))] [/latex]
options.C: [latex] \forall x \forall y [mother(y, x) \to \exists z (mother(z, x) \land \neg noteq(z, y))] [/latex]
options.D: [latex] \forall x \exists y [mother(y, x) \land \neg \exists z (noteq(z, y) \land mother(z, x))] [/latex]

questions.explanation:
We want: for every person [latex]x[/latex], there is exactly one [latex]y[/latex] who is [latex]x[/latex]'s mother — meaning both existence (someone is the mother) and uniqueness (nobody else also qualifies as a distinct mother).

[latex]\forall x\exists y[mother(y,x)\wedge\forall z(noteq(z,y)\to\neg mother(z,x))][/latex]: says "[latex]y[/latex] is a mother of [latex]x[/latex], and every [latex]z[/latex] different from [latex]y[/latex] is not a mother of [latex]x[/latex]" — this correctly captures existence plus uniqueness. Correct.

[latex]\forall x\exists y[mother(y,x)\wedge\neg\exists z(noteq(z,y)\wedge mother(z,x))][/latex]: by De Morgan's law, [latex]\neg\exists z(noteq(z,y)\wedge mother(z,x))[/latex] is logically identical to [latex]\forall z(noteq(z,y)\to\neg mother(z,x))[/latex] — so this is just a different (but equivalent) way of writing the same correct statement above. Correct.

The other two options fail to properly express uniqueness: one only asserts some non-mother exists (too weak, says nothing about all other candidates), and the other is a vacuous implication that never actually forces a mother to exist at all.

Answer: Both the ∀x∃y[...∀z(noteq→¬mother)] form and its De Morgan-equivalent ∀x∃y[...¬∃z(noteq∧mother)] form are correct.

questions.question: Which of the properties hold for the adjacency matrix [latex]A[/latex] of a simple undirected unweighted graph having [latex]n[/latex] vertices?

options.A: The diagonal entries of [latex]A^2[/latex] are the degrees of the vertices of the graph.
options.B: If the graph is connected, then none of the entries of [latex]A^{n-1}+I_n[/latex]can be zero.
options.C: If the sum of all the elements of [latex]A[/latex] is at most 2(n-1), then the graph must be acyclic.
options.D: If there is at least a 1 in each of A's rows and columns, then the graph must be connected.

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- [latex](A^2)_{ii}=\sum_k a_{ik}a_{ki}[/latex] = number of neighbours of i = degree [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Path 1-2-3 (n = 3): [latex]A^2+I[/latex] has entry (1, 2) = 0, since there is no walk of length exactly 2 from 1 to 2 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Sum of entries [latex]\le2(n-1)[/latex] means at most [latex]n-1[/latex] edges. A triangle plus an isolated vertex (n = 4, 3 edges) still has a cycle [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Two disjoint edges on 4 vertices: every row has a 1, but the graph is disconnected [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: The diagonal entries of [latex]A^2[/latex] are the degrees of the vertices

questions.question:
The degree sequence of a simple graph is the sequence of the degrees of the nodes in the graph in decreasing order. Which of the following sequences can not be the degree sequence of any graph?
I. 7, 6, 5, 4, 4, 3, 2, 1
II. 6, 6, 6, 6, 3, 3, 2, 2
III. 7, 6, 6, 4, 4, 3, 2, 2
IV. 8, 7, 7, 6, 4, 2, 1, 1

Checking each statement:
- IV: 8 vertices, so maximum degree is 7. A degree of 8 is impossible.
- II: Havel-Hakimi: 6,6,6,6,3,3,2,2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 5,5,5,2,2,1,2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 5,5,5,2,2,2,1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4,4,1,1,1,1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3,0,0,0,1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3,1,0,0,0. A 3 with only one non-zero vertex left [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] impossible.
- I and III pass the test.

Answer: II and IV

questions.question:
Consider a set U of 23 different compounds in a Chemistry lab. There is a subset S of U of 9 compounds, each of which reacts with exactly 3 compounds of U. Consider the following statements:

I. Each compound in U \ S reacts with an odd number of compounds.
II. At least one compound in U \ S reacts with an odd number of compounds.
III. Each compound in U n S reacts with an even number of compounds.

Which one of the above statements is ALWAYS TRUE?
questions.explanation:
Model compounds as vertices and reactions as edges. The sum of all degrees is even (handshake lemma).

The 9 compounds in S have degree 3 each: total 27 (odd). So the degrees of U \ S must add to an odd number, which needs at least one odd degree there. Nothing forces every one to be odd.

Answer: Only II
